entry.title: Building a Secrets Detection Pre-Commit Hook in 50 Lines
entry.summary: Secrets leaking into git repositories cause a disproportionate share of real-world breaches. AWS keys committed to a public GitHub repo get scraped by bots within minutes — sometimes seconds. The fix is to catch them before they ever reach the commit, not after. CI/CD scanners catch leaks after the fact. The commit is already in history at that point, and you need to rotate the secret, scrub the history with git filter-branch or BFG, and hope no bot grabbed it in the window between push and detection. A pre-commit hook runs locally before the commit lands — zero-latency interception. There are heavy tools like truffleHog, gitleaks, and detect-secrets. They're excellent for large organizations. But if you want something lightweight, auditable, and easy to customize for your team's specific …

entry.title: APA vs. MLA vs. Chicago: A Developer's Guide to Citation Formats (and a Tiny Formatter in TypeScript)
entry.summary: Citation formatting is a strange corner of academic life. The rules are precise, they differ from style to style, and they change between editions. Students lose points for a misplaced period or a missing italic, and the frustration is real because the rules feel arbitrary. To a developer, though, a citation looks very familiar. It's structured data (author, title, year, publisher, URL) rendered through a template. Different styles are just different templates operating on the same fields. Once you see it that way, the whole thing becomes a lot less mysterious, and you can reason about it the same way you'd reason about a serializer. entry.summary:
AI Workloads Push Cooling Limits
AI training clusters now routinely push rack densities well beyond the levels that traditional air-cooled designs were built to handle. These concentrated compute loads generate intense heat that demands far greater cooling capacity, placing simultaneous strain on both electricity supply and water infrastructure in data center regions. Evaporative cooling systems have long offered an efficient way to reject this heat, yet their reliance on large volumes of water creates growing tension with local resource constraints. entry.title: Claude Code docs pages changed on the day we read them
entry.summary: Claude Code documentation pages keep changing under a book that cites them. On 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-15 our KDP package rebuild for book #220 raised the same warning three times: 7 'Check it yourself' boxes needed to be read again because the page they cite was modified on the day of our reading or later. The affected pages are all on code.claude.com. Chapter 3 cites the Agent SDK subagents page. Chapter 5 cites the claude-directory page and the skills page. Chapter 6 cites the monitoring-usage page and the Agent SDK observability page. Chapter 7 cites the tool-search page. The alert text is cut off in the record we have, so we cannot list all 7 boxes here. In most of the listed cases the page was read on 2026-10-14 and changed on 2026-10-14, the same day. The alert says to check whether the change came before or after the reading, and a date alone does not settle that. One observability entry shows a read on 2026-10-14 and a change on 2026-10-15, which is plainly after the read. The alert fired at 2026-10-14 22:08, again at 22:11, and again at 2026-10-15 04:55. The monitoring-usage page was listed at 22:11, and the visible part of the 04:55 alert lists the observability page in that slot instead. The record does not say why, and it does not say what changed on any of these pages. The book is not at KDP yet. The alert fires during the package rebuild, before the file goes out, and it asks for each flagged box to be re-read against its page first. A documentation page's last-modified date has only day resolution, so when it equals the day you read it you cannot tell which version you read; record the time of reading, or read again before you publish. Originally published at neuragrowth.co. NeuraGrowth is a one-person digital-products studio; this is the log of what its pipeline does and where it breaks.
